    Markov Gaussian Processes — Matern Kernels in State-Space Form¶

    This notebook is the first installment of pyrox's Markov-GP track. It introduces MaternSDE — the state-space representation of the Matern-$\nu$ kernel for $\nu \in \{1/2, 3/2, 5/2\}$ — and verifies, end-to-end, that the SDE formulation and the dense kernel describe the same Gaussian process. Once a kernel is in state-space form, GP inference on a 1-D grid drops from $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ Cholesky to $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$ Kalman filtering, where $d \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ is the SDE state dimension.

    Subsequent notebooks (issues #37 finish, #38) will compose SDE kernels, run Kalman / RTS smoothing, and expose MarkovGPPrior for NumPyro models. This one stays focused on the representation layer: math, identities, and visual sanity checks.

    Background — from kernel to SDE¶

    Any stationary GP kernel $k(\tau)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ whose spectral density is rational in $\omega^2$ admits an exact, finite-dimensional state-space representation as a linear time-invariant SDE

    $$d\mathbf{x}(t) = F\,\mathbf{x}(t)\,dt + L\,dw(t), \qquad f(t) = H\,\mathbf{x}(t),$$

    with white-noise driver $w(t)$ of spectral density $Q_c$ and stationary state covariance $P_\infty$ solving the continuous Lyapunov equation

    $$F P_\infty + P_\infty F^\top + L Q_c L^\top = 0.$$

    Discretising at non-uniform observation times $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_N$ with $\Delta t_k = t_{k+1} - t_k$ gives the discrete-time linear-Gaussian model

    $$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A_k \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{q}_k, \qquad \mathbf{q}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_k), \qquad f_k = H\,\mathbf{x}_k,$$

    with $A_k = \exp(F\,\Delta t_k)$ and $Q_k = P_\infty - A_k P_\infty A_k^\top$. The recovered continuous autocovariance is $k(\tau) = H \exp(F\tau) P_\infty H^\top$ for $\tau \geq 0$, which we will verify against the dense Matern kernel below.

    Matern-$\nu$ companion form¶

    For Matern-$\nu$ with $\nu = p + 1/2$ and $\lambda = \sqrt{2\nu}/\ell$, the state has dimension $d = p + 1$ and $F$ is the companion matrix of $(\lambda + s)^d$. Concretely:

    Order $p$ $\nu$ $d$ $\lambda$ Closed-form kernel
    0 1/2 1 $1/\ell$ $\sigma^2 \exp(-r/\ell)$
    1 3/2 2 $\sqrt{3}/\ell$ $\sigma^2 (1 + \sqrt{3} r/\ell)\exp(-\sqrt{3} r/\ell)$
    2 5/2 3 $\sqrt{5}/\ell$ $\sigma^2 (1 + \sqrt{5} r/\ell + 5 r^2/(3\ell^2))\exp(-\sqrt{5} r/\ell)$

    MaternSDE ships these three orders. Composition rules (sum / product), CosineSDE, PeriodicSDE, and the Kalman-based MarkovGPPrior follow in subsequent PRs.

    1. Inspecting the SDE parameters¶

    A MaternSDE(variance, lengthscale, order) produces a closed-form $(F, L, H, Q_c, P_\infty)$ tuple via sde_params(). We instantiate one kernel per order and print the structural matrices alongside two structural identities:

    1. Variance recovery: $H P_\infty H^\top = \sigma^2$.
    2. Lyapunov closure: $F P_\infty + P_\infty F^\top + L Q_c L^\top = 0$.
    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    sigma2 = 1.0
ell = 0.5
sdes = {p: MaternSDE(variance=sigma2, lengthscale=ell, order=p) for p in (0, 1, 2)}

for p, sde in sdes.items():
    F, L, H, Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    var_rec = float((H @ P_inf @ H.T).squeeze())

    Both invariants hold to machine precision in float64. The variance-recovery identity says the SDE state encodes the GP value plus $d-1$ derivative-like coordinates; the Lyapunov identity says the stationary state covariance is consistent with the drift $F$ and the diffusion $L Q_c L^\top$.

    2. SDE autocovariance vs. dense Matern kernel¶

    The continuous-time stationary autocovariance recovered from the SDE is

    $$k_{\text{SDE}}(\tau) \;=\; H\,\exp(F \tau)\,P_\infty\,H^\top, \qquad \tau \geq 0.$$

    This must equal the dense Matern Gram value at lag $\tau$. We compute both on a fine grid and overlay them.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    def sde_autocov(sde: MaternSDE, taus: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()

    def _k(tau: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
        return (H @ jsl.expm(F * tau) @ P_inf @ H.T).squeeze()

    return jax.vmap(_k)(taus)


taus = jnp.linspace(0.0, 2.5, 201)
X = taus[:, None]
X0 = jnp.zeros((1, 1))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 3.6), sharey=True)
for ax, (p, sde) in zip(axes, sdes.items(), strict=False):
    k_sde = sde_autocov(sde, taus)
    k_dense = matern_kernel(
        X, X0, jnp.asarray(sigma2), jnp.asarray(ell), nu=p + 0.5
    ).squeeze()
    ax.plot(taus, k_dense, label="dense Matern", lw=2.4, alpha=0.85)
    ax.plot(taus, k_sde, "--", label=r"$H \exp(F\tau) P_\infty H^\top$", lw=1.7)
    err = float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(k_sde - k_dense)))
    ax.set_title(rf"Matern-{2 * sde.order + 1}/2 (max abs err: {err:.1e})")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"lag $\tau$")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$k(\tau)$")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
fig.suptitle("SDE autocovariance recovers the dense Matern kernel")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    def sde_autocov(sde: MaternSDE, taus: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray: F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params() def _k(tau: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray: return (H @ jsl.expm(F * tau) @ P_inf @ H.T).squeeze() return jax.vmap(_k)(taus) taus = jnp.linspace(0.0, 2.5, 201) X = taus[:, None] X0 = jnp.zeros((1, 1)) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 3.6), sharey=True) for ax, (p, sde) in zip(axes, sdes.items(), strict=False): k_sde = sde_autocov(sde, taus) k_dense = matern_kernel( X, X0, jnp.asarray(sigma2), jnp.asarray(ell), nu=p + 0.5 ).squeeze() ax.plot(taus, k_dense, label="dense Matern", lw=2.4, alpha=0.85) ax.plot(taus, k_sde, "--", label=r"$H \exp(F\tau) P_\infty H^\top$", lw=1.7) err = float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(k_sde - k_dense))) ax.set_title(rf"Matern-{2 * sde.order + 1}/2 (max abs err: {err:.1e})") ax.set_xlabel(r"lag $\tau$") ax.grid(alpha=0.25) axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$k(\tau)$") axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right") fig.suptitle("SDE autocovariance recovers the dense Matern kernel") fig.tight_layout() plt.show()

    All three orders agree to numerical precision. The SDE is not an approximation of the Matern kernel — for $\nu \in \{1/2, 3/2, 5/2\}$ it is an exact reformulation.

    3. Discretisation: $A_k$ and $Q_k$ as functions of $\Delta t$¶

    Given a time step $\Delta t$, the discrete-time transition is $A(\Delta t) = \exp(F\,\Delta t)$ and the process-noise covariance is $Q(\Delta t) = P_\infty - A(\Delta t) P_\infty A(\Delta t)^\top$. Two endpoints are worth checking:

    • As $\Delta t \to 0$, $A \to I$ and $Q \to 0$ (no time elapsed, no uncertainty added).
    • As $\Delta t \to \infty$, $A P_\infty A^\top \to 0$ (the dynamics decay back to the stationary distribution) and so $Q \to P_\infty$ (the next state is independent of the previous one and has the stationary distribution).

    We plot $\|A(\Delta t)\|_2$ and the trace of $Q(\Delta t)$ over a log-spaced range of step sizes.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    dts = jnp.geomspace(1e-3, 5e1, 200)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
for p, sde in sdes.items():
    A, Q = sde.discretise_sequence(dts)
    A_norm = jnp.linalg.norm(A, ord=2, axis=(1, 2))
    Q_trace = jnp.einsum("nii->n", Q)
    _, _, _, _, P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    P_inf_trace = float(jnp.trace(P_inf))
    label = rf"$\nu = {p}+1/2$"
    axes[0].plot(dts, A_norm, label=label, lw=1.8)
    axes[1].plot(dts, Q_trace, label=label, lw=1.8)
    axes[1].axhline(
        P_inf_trace, color=axes[1].lines[-1].get_color(), ls=":", alpha=0.55
    )

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"step size $\Delta t$")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\|A(\Delta t)\|_2$")
axes[0].set_title(r"Transition matrix decay: $A \to 0$ as $\Delta t \to \infty$")
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\mathrm{tr}\,Q(\Delta t)$")
axes[1].set_title(r"Process noise growth: $Q \to P_\infty$ as $\Delta t \to \infty$")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    dts = jnp.geomspace(1e-3, 5e1, 200) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6)) for p, sde in sdes.items(): A, Q = sde.discretise_sequence(dts) A_norm = jnp.linalg.norm(A, ord=2, axis=(1, 2)) Q_trace = jnp.einsum("nii->n", Q) _, _, _, _, P_inf = sde.sde_params() P_inf_trace = float(jnp.trace(P_inf)) label = rf"$\nu = {p}+1/2$" axes[0].plot(dts, A_norm, label=label, lw=1.8) axes[1].plot(dts, Q_trace, label=label, lw=1.8) axes[1].axhline( P_inf_trace, color=axes[1].lines[-1].get_color(), ls=":", alpha=0.55 ) for ax in axes: ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_xlabel(r"step size $\Delta t$") ax.grid(alpha=0.25) axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\|A(\Delta t)\|_2$") axes[0].set_title(r"Transition matrix decay: $A \to 0$ as $\Delta t \to \infty$") axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\mathrm{tr}\,Q(\Delta t)$") axes[1].set_title(r"Process noise growth: $Q \to P_\infty$ as $\Delta t \to \infty$") axes[1].legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right") fig.tight_layout() plt.show()

    Dotted horizontal lines mark $\mathrm{tr}\,P_\infty$ for each order — the asymptote $Q$ relaxes onto. Higher-order Materns relax slower (more oscillatory state coordinates carry inertia), but the limit is the same.

    4. Sample paths via forward simulation of the discrete-time SDE¶

    We can draw GP sample paths without ever forming a dense Gram matrix. The recipe is the standard linear-Gaussian forward simulation of the discrete state-space model:

    1. Sample $\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, P_\infty)$.
    2. For $k = 0, 1, \dots, N-1$: sample $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A_k \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{q}_k$ with $\mathbf{q}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_k)$.
    3. Read out $f_k = H\,\mathbf{x}_k$.

    All work is local in time; no $N \times N$ Cholesky. We compare paths drawn this way against paths drawn from the dense Matern Cholesky for the same time grid.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    def sample_sde_paths(
    sde: MaternSDE,
    times: jnp.ndarray,
    n_paths: int,
    key: jax.Array,
) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Forward-simulate ``n_paths`` realisations of the discrete state-space model."""
    _F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    d = sde.state_dim
    dts = jnp.diff(times)
    A_all, Q_all = sde.discretise_sequence(dts)
    L_inf = jnp.linalg.cholesky(P_inf + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(d))
    L_step = jnp.linalg.cholesky(Q_all + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(d)[None])

    key_init, key_step = jr.split(key)
    x0 = L_inf @ jr.normal(key_init, (d, n_paths))  # (d, n_paths)
    eps = jr.normal(key_step, (dts.shape[0], d, n_paths))

    def step(
        x_prev: jnp.ndarray, inputs: tuple[jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray]
    ) -> tuple[jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray]:
        A_k, L_k, eps_k = inputs
        x_next = A_k @ x_prev + L_k @ eps_k
        return x_next, x_next

    _, xs = jax.lax.scan(step, x0, (A_all, L_step, eps))
    states = jnp.concatenate([x0[None], xs], axis=0)  # (N, d, n_paths)
    f_paths = jnp.einsum("ij,njp->np", H, states)  # (N, n_paths)
    return f_paths


def sample_dense_paths(
    sde: MaternSDE,
    times: jnp.ndarray,
    n_paths: int,
    key: jax.Array,
) -> jnp.ndarray:
    X = times[:, None]
    K = matern_kernel(X, X, sde.variance, sde.lengthscale, nu=sde.order + 0.5)
    K = K + 1e-8 * jnp.eye(X.shape[0])
    L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(K)
    return L @ jr.normal(key, (X.shape[0], n_paths))


N = 320
times = jnp.linspace(0.0, 4.0, N)
n_paths = 4
seed = 0

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5), sharex=True)
for row, (_p, sde) in enumerate(sdes.items()):
    sde_paths = sample_sde_paths(sde, times, n_paths, jr.PRNGKey(seed))
    dense_paths = sample_dense_paths(sde, times, n_paths, jr.PRNGKey(seed + 1))
    for j in range(n_paths):
        axes[row, 0].plot(times, sde_paths[:, j], lw=1.2, alpha=0.85)
        axes[row, 1].plot(times, dense_paths[:, j], lw=1.2, alpha=0.85)
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(rf"Matern-{2 * sde.order + 1}/2")
    for ax in axes[row]:
        ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
        ax.axhline(0.0, color="k", lw=0.4, alpha=0.4)
axes[0, 0].set_title("SDE forward-simulation paths")
axes[0, 1].set_title("Dense Matern Cholesky paths")
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("t")
fig.suptitle("Same statistics, different generation path")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    def sample_sde_paths( sde: MaternSDE, times: jnp.ndarray, n_paths: int, key: jax.Array, ) -> jnp.ndarray: """Forward-simulate ``n_paths`` realisations of the discrete state-space model.""" _F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params() d = sde.state_dim dts = jnp.diff(times) A_all, Q_all = sde.discretise_sequence(dts) L_inf = jnp.linalg.cholesky(P_inf + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(d)) L_step = jnp.linalg.cholesky(Q_all + 1e-10 * jnp.eye(d)[None]) key_init, key_step = jr.split(key) x0 = L_inf @ jr.normal(key_init, (d, n_paths)) # (d, n_paths) eps = jr.normal(key_step, (dts.shape[0], d, n_paths)) def step( x_prev: jnp.ndarray, inputs: tuple[jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray] ) -> tuple[jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray]: A_k, L_k, eps_k = inputs x_next = A_k @ x_prev + L_k @ eps_k return x_next, x_next _, xs = jax.lax.scan(step, x0, (A_all, L_step, eps)) states = jnp.concatenate([x0[None], xs], axis=0) # (N, d, n_paths) f_paths = jnp.einsum("ij,njp->np", H, states) # (N, n_paths) return f_paths def sample_dense_paths( sde: MaternSDE, times: jnp.ndarray, n_paths: int, key: jax.Array, ) -> jnp.ndarray: X = times[:, None] K = matern_kernel(X, X, sde.variance, sde.lengthscale, nu=sde.order + 0.5) K = K + 1e-8 * jnp.eye(X.shape[0]) L = jnp.linalg.cholesky(K) return L @ jr.normal(key, (X.shape[0], n_paths)) N = 320 times = jnp.linspace(0.0, 4.0, N) n_paths = 4 seed = 0 fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5), sharex=True) for row, (_p, sde) in enumerate(sdes.items()): sde_paths = sample_sde_paths(sde, times, n_paths, jr.PRNGKey(seed)) dense_paths = sample_dense_paths(sde, times, n_paths, jr.PRNGKey(seed + 1)) for j in range(n_paths): axes[row, 0].plot(times, sde_paths[:, j], lw=1.2, alpha=0.85) axes[row, 1].plot(times, dense_paths[:, j], lw=1.2, alpha=0.85) axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(rf"Matern-{2 * sde.order + 1}/2") for ax in axes[row]: ax.grid(alpha=0.2) ax.axhline(0.0, color="k", lw=0.4, alpha=0.4) axes[0, 0].set_title("SDE forward-simulation paths") axes[0, 1].set_title("Dense Matern Cholesky paths") for ax in axes[-1]: ax.set_xlabel("t") fig.suptitle("Same statistics, different generation path") fig.tight_layout() plt.show()

    Each row pairs the same kernel order; the seeds differ across columns so the realisations are independent draws. Visually the rougher Matern-1/2 paths sit on top, the smoother Matern-5/2 paths at the bottom, with the SDE and dense columns indistinguishable in their statistical character. The variances and correlation lengths match by construction.

    5. Empirical covariance of SDE samples matches the analytic kernel¶

    A stronger check than visual matching: estimate the covariance $\hat C_{ij} = \mathrm{Cov}[f(t_i), f(t_j)]$ from many SDE-simulated paths and compare to the closed-form Matern Gram on the same grid.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    n_mc = 2000
mc_times = jnp.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 41)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 4.0))
for ax, (p, sde) in zip(axes, sdes.items(), strict=False):
    paths = sample_sde_paths(sde, mc_times, n_mc, jr.PRNGKey(11 + p))  # (N, n_mc)
    paths_centered = paths - paths.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    C_emp = (paths_centered @ paths_centered.T) / (n_mc - 1)
    K_true = matern_kernel(
        mc_times[:, None],
        mc_times[:, None],
        sde.variance,
        sde.lengthscale,
        nu=sde.order + 0.5,
    )
    ax.plot(
        mc_times, jnp.diag(C_emp), label=r"$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\,f(t)$ (MC)", lw=1.7
    )
    ax.plot(mc_times, jnp.diag(K_true), "--", label=r"$\sigma^2$", lw=1.4)
    ax.plot(
        mc_times,
        C_emp[:, 0],
        lw=1.7,
        label=r"$\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}\,(f(0), f(t))$ (MC)",
    )
    ax.plot(mc_times, K_true[:, 0], "--", lw=1.4, label=r"$k(t, 0)$")
    ax.set_title(rf"Matern-{2 * sde.order + 1}/2  ({n_mc} paths)")
    ax.set_xlabel("t")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle(
    "Empirical covariance from SDE samples agrees with the analytic Matern kernel"
)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    n_mc = 2000 mc_times = jnp.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 41) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 4.0)) for ax, (p, sde) in zip(axes, sdes.items(), strict=False): paths = sample_sde_paths(sde, mc_times, n_mc, jr.PRNGKey(11 + p)) # (N, n_mc) paths_centered = paths - paths.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) C_emp = (paths_centered @ paths_centered.T) / (n_mc - 1) K_true = matern_kernel( mc_times[:, None], mc_times[:, None], sde.variance, sde.lengthscale, nu=sde.order + 0.5, ) ax.plot( mc_times, jnp.diag(C_emp), label=r"$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\,f(t)$ (MC)", lw=1.7 ) ax.plot(mc_times, jnp.diag(K_true), "--", label=r"$\sigma^2$", lw=1.4) ax.plot( mc_times, C_emp[:, 0], lw=1.7, label=r"$\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}\,(f(0), f(t))$ (MC)", ) ax.plot(mc_times, K_true[:, 0], "--", lw=1.4, label=r"$k(t, 0)$") ax.set_title(rf"Matern-{2 * sde.order + 1}/2 ({n_mc} paths)") ax.set_xlabel("t") ax.grid(alpha=0.25) axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=8) fig.suptitle( "Empirical covariance from SDE samples agrees with the analytic Matern kernel" ) fig.tight_layout() plt.show()

    Solid lines are Monte-Carlo estimates from $n_\text{mc} = 2000$ forward simulations; dashed lines are the closed-form values. They overlap to the precision afforded by 2000 samples.

    6. The kernel zoo — primitives and composition rules¶

    Matern alone is enough to cover smooth time series, but real signals usually have more structure: a fixed offset, a carrier oscillation, an annual cycle, a quasi-periodic modulation. State-space form scales gracefully here too — every additional kernel is another small block in the state, not another factor of $N$ in inference cost.

    This section walks through the four new primitive / composition kernels added on top of MaternSDE:

    Class Math State dim
    ConstantSDE(σ²) $k(\tau) = \sigma^2$ 1
    CosineSDE(σ², ω) $k(\tau) = \sigma^2 \cos(\omega\,\tau)$ 2
    PeriodicSDE(σ², ℓ, T, J) MacKay periodic, Fourier-truncated to $J$ harmonics $1 + 2J$
    SumSDE((k₁, …)) $k(\tau) = \sum_i k_i(\tau)$ $\sum_i d_i$
    ProductSDE(k₁, k₂) $k(\tau) = k_1(\tau)\,k_2(\tau)$ $d_1 \cdot d_2$
    QuasiPeriodicSDE(matern, periodic) thin wrapper for ProductSDE $d_M (1 + 2J)$

    SumSDE is block-diagonal in $F$, $L$, $Q_c$ and $P_\infty$, with the readouts $H$ concatenated. ProductSDE uses Kronecker-sum drift $F = F_1 \otimes I + I \otimes F_2$ and Kronecker-product readout / stationary covariance $H = H_1 \otimes H_2$, $P_\infty = P_{\infty,1} \otimes P_{\infty,2}$. The diffusion is a sum of two Kronecker terms — see the ProductSDE docstring for the full formula.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    from kernellib.functional import periodic_kernel
from pyrox_ssm import (
    ConstantSDE,
    CosineSDE,
    PeriodicSDE,
    ProductSDE,
    QuasiPeriodicSDE,
    SumSDE,
)
    from kernellib.functional import periodic_kernel from pyrox_ssm import ( ConstantSDE, CosineSDE, PeriodicSDE, ProductSDE, QuasiPeriodicSDE, SumSDE, )

    6.1 Building blocks: ConstantSDE, CosineSDE, PeriodicSDE¶

    We instantiate one of each, draw a few sample paths via the same forward-simulation recipe used for Matern in §4, and overlay the SDE autocovariance against a dense reference where one is available. PeriodicSDE uses n_harmonics = 7 — enough to match the MacKay periodic kernel to better than 1e-4 in the typical hyperparameter regime.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    const = ConstantSDE(variance=0.6)
cos = CosineSDE(variance=1.0, frequency=2.0 * jnp.pi)  # period 1
per = PeriodicSDE(variance=1.0, lengthscale=1.0, period=1.0, n_harmonics=7)

primitives = {"ConstantSDE": const, "CosineSDE": cos, "PeriodicSDE": per}

times_demo = jnp.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 320)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(13, 7.8), sharex="col")
for row, (name, sde) in enumerate(primitives.items()):
    paths = sample_sde_paths(sde, times_demo, n_paths=4, key=jr.PRNGKey(7 + row))
    for j in range(4):
        axes[row, 0].plot(times_demo, paths[:, j], lw=1.1, alpha=0.85)
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(name)
    axes[row, 0].grid(alpha=0.25)
    axes[row, 0].axhline(0.0, color="k", lw=0.4, alpha=0.4)

    F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    taus_demo = jnp.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 401)
    K_sde = jax.vmap(
        lambda t, F=F, H=H, P_inf=P_inf: (H @ jsl.expm(F * t) @ P_inf @ H.T).squeeze()
    )(taus_demo)
    axes[row, 1].plot(taus_demo, K_sde, lw=1.8, label="SDE autocov", color="C0")
    if name == "ConstantSDE":
        axes[row, 1].axhline(0.6, ls="--", lw=1.3, color="C3", label=r"$\sigma^2$")
    elif name == "CosineSDE":
        axes[row, 1].plot(
            taus_demo,
            jnp.cos(2.0 * jnp.pi * taus_demo),
            "--",
            lw=1.3,
            label=r"$\sigma^2 \cos(\omega\tau)$",
        )
    else:
        K_dense = periodic_kernel(
            taus_demo[:, None],
            jnp.zeros((1, 1)),
            jnp.asarray(1.0),
            jnp.asarray(1.0),
            jnp.asarray(1.0),
        ).squeeze()
        axes[row, 1].plot(taus_demo, K_dense, "--", lw=1.3, label="MacKay periodic")
    axes[row, 1].grid(alpha=0.25)
    axes[row, 1].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
axes[0, 0].set_title("Sample paths")
axes[0, 1].set_title("Autocovariance vs reference")
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("t" if ax is axes[-1, 0] else r"lag $\tau$")
fig.suptitle("Primitive SDE kernels: paths and autocovariance")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    const = ConstantSDE(variance=0.6) cos = CosineSDE(variance=1.0, frequency=2.0 * jnp.pi) # period 1 per = PeriodicSDE(variance=1.0, lengthscale=1.0, period=1.0, n_harmonics=7) primitives = {"ConstantSDE": const, "CosineSDE": cos, "PeriodicSDE": per} times_demo = jnp.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 320) fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(13, 7.8), sharex="col") for row, (name, sde) in enumerate(primitives.items()): paths = sample_sde_paths(sde, times_demo, n_paths=4, key=jr.PRNGKey(7 + row)) for j in range(4): axes[row, 0].plot(times_demo, paths[:, j], lw=1.1, alpha=0.85) axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(name) axes[row, 0].grid(alpha=0.25) axes[row, 0].axhline(0.0, color="k", lw=0.4, alpha=0.4) F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = sde.sde_params() taus_demo = jnp.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 401) K_sde = jax.vmap( lambda t, F=F, H=H, P_inf=P_inf: (H @ jsl.expm(F * t) @ P_inf @ H.T).squeeze() )(taus_demo) axes[row, 1].plot(taus_demo, K_sde, lw=1.8, label="SDE autocov", color="C0") if name == "ConstantSDE": axes[row, 1].axhline(0.6, ls="--", lw=1.3, color="C3", label=r"$\sigma^2$") elif name == "CosineSDE": axes[row, 1].plot( taus_demo, jnp.cos(2.0 * jnp.pi * taus_demo), "--", lw=1.3, label=r"$\sigma^2 \cos(\omega\tau)$", ) else: K_dense = periodic_kernel( taus_demo[:, None], jnp.zeros((1, 1)), jnp.asarray(1.0), jnp.asarray(1.0), jnp.asarray(1.0), ).squeeze() axes[row, 1].plot(taus_demo, K_dense, "--", lw=1.3, label="MacKay periodic") axes[row, 1].grid(alpha=0.25) axes[row, 1].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=8) axes[0, 0].set_title("Sample paths") axes[0, 1].set_title("Autocovariance vs reference") for ax in axes[-1]: ax.set_xlabel("t" if ax is axes[-1, 0] else r"lag $\tau$") fig.suptitle("Primitive SDE kernels: paths and autocovariance") fig.tight_layout() plt.show()
    • ConstantSDE paths are flat realisations: each draw is a single Gaussian random variable replicated across time. The autocovariance is the constant $\sigma^2$.
    • CosineSDE paths are pure sinusoids with random amplitude and phase. The covariance oscillates exactly as $\sigma^2 \cos(\omega\tau)$.
    • PeriodicSDE paths are smooth, period-aware, and not sinusoidal — they live in the function space of the MacKay periodic kernel. Truncating the Fourier expansion at $J=7$ matches the dense kernel within plotting precision.

    6.2 Composition: trend + offset via SumSDE¶

    A common modelling pattern is "smooth trend on top of a fixed offset". With dense kernels this is one line: RBF + Constant. In state-space form it's exactly the same — just SumSDE. The block-diagonal construction keeps each component's state space disjoint, so the cost is purely additive ($\sum_i d_i$).

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    trend = SumSDE(
    (
        MaternSDE(variance=0.7, lengthscale=0.8, order=1),
        ConstantSDE(variance=0.4),
    )
)
print(f"SumSDE state dim: {trend.state_dim}  (= 2 + 1)")

paths = sample_sde_paths(trend, times_demo, n_paths=6, key=jr.PRNGKey(33))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for j in range(6):
    axes[0].plot(times_demo, paths[:, j], lw=1.1, alpha=0.85)
axes[0].set_title("MaternSDE-3/2 + ConstantSDE — sample paths")
axes[0].set_xlabel("t")
axes[0].grid(alpha=0.25)

F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = trend.sde_params()
taus_demo = jnp.linspace(0.0, 3.0, 301)
K_sum = jax.vmap(lambda t: (H @ jsl.expm(F * t) @ P_inf @ H.T).squeeze())(taus_demo)
K_truth = (
    matern_kernel(
        taus_demo[:, None],
        jnp.zeros((1, 1)),
        jnp.asarray(0.7),
        jnp.asarray(0.8),
        nu=1.5,
    ).squeeze()
    + 0.4
)
axes[1].plot(taus_demo, K_sum, lw=2.2, label=r"$H \exp(F\tau) P_\infty H^\top$")
axes[1].plot(taus_demo, K_truth, "--", lw=1.3, label=r"$k_M(\tau) + \sigma_C^2$")

axes[1].set_xlabel(r"lag $\tau$")
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.25)
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")

plt.show()

    Sample paths show the Matern wiggle riding on independently-drawn constant offsets — exactly the prior we wanted. The autocovariance recovers $k_{\rm Matern}(\tau) + \sigma_C^2$ to machine precision.

    6.3 Composition: damped oscillation via ProductSDE¶

    The product of a Matern and a Cosine is the subband Matern kernel — a stationary kernel whose spectral density is centred on a non-zero carrier $\omega_0$. It's the right prior for narrowband oscillatory signals (audio harmonics, geophysical resonances, modulated sensor traces). State dim is $d_M \cdot d_C$ — for Matern-3/2 × Cosine that's $2 \cdot 2 = 4$.

    In [12]:
    Copied!

    MaternSDE(variance=1.0, lengthscale=0.6, order=1),
    CosineSDE(variance=1.0, frequency=2.0 * jnp.pi * 1.5),  # 1.5 Hz carrier
)
print(f"ProductSDE state dim: {damped.state_dim}")

paths = sample_sde_paths(damped, times_demo, n_paths=4, key=jr.PRNGKey(101))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for j in range(4):
    axes[0].plot(times_demo, paths[:, j], lw=1.1, alpha=0.85)
axes[0].set_title("MaternSDE-3/2 x CosineSDE — sample paths")
axes[0].set_xlabel("t")
axes[0].grid(alpha=0.25)

F, _L, H, _Q_c, P_inf = damped.sde_params()
taus_demo = jnp.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 401)

K_m = matern_kernel(
    taus_demo[:, None], jnp.zeros((1, 1)), jnp.asarray(1.0), jnp.asarray(0.6), nu=1.5
).squeeze()
K_c = jnp.cos(2.0 * jnp.pi * 1.5 * taus_demo)
axes[1].plot(taus_demo, K_prod, lw=2.2, label=r"ProductSDE autocov")
axes[1].plot(
    taus_demo,
    K_m * K_c,
    "--",
    lw=1.3,
    label=r"$k_{\rm Matern}(\tau)\,\cos(\omega_0\tau)$",
)
axes[1].set_title("Autocovariance: ProductSDE matches dense product")
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"lag $\tau$")
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.25)
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")

    ProductSDE state dim: 4

    The paths are oscillations whose envelope drifts on the Matern lengthscale — a damped carrier signal. The product autocovariance matches $k_M(\tau) \cos(\omega_0 \tau)$ to numerical precision (the slight curvature of the envelope reflects the Matern factor).

    6.4 Quasi-periodic kernels — modulated periodic structure¶

    The classic "stellar" prior: a periodic signal whose amplitude drifts slowly over time. Mathematically it's $k_{\rm Matern}(\tau) \cdot k_{\rm Periodic}(\tau)$ — a ProductSDE of two stationary kernels. QuasiPeriodicSDE is just a thin convenience wrapper that documents the standard recipe.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    qp = QuasiPeriodicSDE(
    MaternSDE(variance=1.0, lengthscale=2.5, order=1),  # slow envelope (long ell)
    PeriodicSDE(variance=1.0, lengthscale=1.0, period=0.6, n_harmonics=5),
)
print(f"QuasiPeriodicSDE state dim: {qp.state_dim}  (= 2 * (1 + 2*5))")

    Each draw shows a clear period of about 0.6 time units, but the amplitude drifts on a slow Matern timescale — short bursts of high-amplitude oscillation followed by quiescent stretches, exactly the prior class used for stellar light curves and modulated seasonal signals.

    7. From the kernel zoo to geoscience signals¶

    Section 6 showed that every class above is an exact state-space kernel. This section is about when to reach for each one. The useful question is rarely "which kernel is best" but three narrower ones: what does the variable's power spectrum look like, along which axis (time, a transect, a spatial field) is the kernel defined, and how was the variable sampled. We read each class through its spectrum, map it to geophysical signals where the literature motivates that choice, and end with the successes and failures to look out for.

    7.1 Every SDE kernel is a statement about a spectrum¶

    A stationary SDE $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} = F\,\mathbf{x}\,\mathrm{d}t + L\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ with readout $f = H\mathbf{x}$ is a linear filter driven by white noise, so its output has the power spectral density

    $$S(\omega) = H\,(i\omega I - F)^{-1}\,L\,Q_c\,L^\top\,(i\omega I - F)^{-\mathsf{H}}\,H^\top,$$

    and the Wiener–Khinchin theorem returns the kernel as $k(\tau) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int S(\omega)\,e^{i\omega\tau}\,\mathrm{d}\omega$ (Särkkä & Solin, 2019). Three facts follow, and they are most of what you need to choose a kernel.

    • Matern sets a knee and a slope. For Matern-$\nu$, $S(\omega) \propto (\lambda^2 + \omega^2)^{-(\nu + 1/2)}$ with $\lambda = \sqrt{2\nu}/\ell$. The spectrum is flat below the knee $\omega \approx \lambda$ and falls as $\omega^{-(2\nu+1)}$ above it: slopes of $-2$, $-4$ and $-6$ for orders $p = 0, 1, 2$. The lengthscale places the knee; the order sets how fast high-frequency variance dies, which is the same thing as how many derivatives the paths have.
    • Sums add spectra. SumSDE puts each component's variance in its own band, which is why decompositions such as trend + seasonal cycle + anomaly are natural in this form.
    • Products move spectra. Multiplying a kernel by $\cos(\omega_0\tau)$ convolves its spectrum with lines at $\pm\omega_0$, so ProductSDE(MaternSDE, CosineSDE) is a band centred on $\omega_0$ whose width is set by the Matern knee $\lambda$. QuasiPeriodicSDE places one such band at every harmonic $j\omega_0$. CosineSDE, PeriodicSDE and ConstantSDE on their own carry no diffusion ($Q_c = 0$): all their variance sits on exact lines at $\omega_0$, at $j\omega_0$, or at $\omega = 0$.

    The helper below evaluates $S(\omega)$ from sde_params() directly and checks two of these facts numerically: that $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int S\,\mathrm{d}\omega$ recovers the Matern variance, and that the spectrum of a SumSDE equals the sum of its components' spectra.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    def sde_psd(sde, omegas: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
    """Power spectral density of a stationary SDE kernel at angular frequencies ``omegas``."""
    F, L, H, Q_c, _P_inf = sde.sde_params()
    d = F.shape[0]
    LQL = L @ jnp.atleast_2d(Q_c) @ L.T

    def one(w: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
        G = jnp.linalg.solve(1j * w * jnp.eye(d) - F, jnp.eye(d))
        return jnp.real(H @ G @ LQL @ G.conj().T @ H.T).squeeze()

    return jax.vmap(one)(omegas)


omega_grid = jnp.linspace(-2000.0, 2000.0, 800_001)
for p in (0, 1, 2):
    sde = MaternSDE(variance=sigma2, lengthscale=ell, order=p)
    var = jnp.trapezoid(sde_psd(sde, omega_grid), omega_grid) / (2.0 * jnp.pi)
    print(
        f"Matern-{2 * p + 1}/2: (1/2pi) * integral of S = {float(var):.4f}  (variance = {sigma2})"
    )

    7.2 Which class for which signal¶

    Class Spectrum Reach for it when Geoscience example Literature
    MaternSDE, order 0 (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck) flat, then $\omega^{-2}$ the signal is rough and mean-reverting with one memory time $\ell$ SST anomalies integrating weather noise; the red-noise null hypothesis for climate spectra Hasselmann (1976); Frankignoul & Hasselmann (1977)
    MaternSDE, orders 1 and 2 flat, then $\omega^{-4}$ or $\omega^{-6}$ the paths should be once or twice differentiable; the default for smooth physical fields a slowly varying trend; interpolating a smooth state between sparse observations Stein (1999); Rasmussen & Williams (2006)
    ConstantSDE all variance at $\omega = 0$ a level that is unknown but fixed over the record a station, instrument or retrieval offset —
    SumSDE of CosineSDEs lines at known $\omega_k$ the frequencies are fixed by physics and only amplitude and phase are unknown tidal constituents M2, S2, K1, O1 in a tide-gauge or altimetry record Pawlowicz et al. (2002)
    PeriodicSDE lines at $j\omega_0$ a cycle repeats with a fixed, non-sinusoidal shape a climatological diurnal or seasonal cycle Solin & Särkkä (2014)
    QuasiPeriodicSDE bands at $j\omega_0$ the cycle repeats but its amplitude and shape drift the seasonal cycle of atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa Rasmussen & Williams (2006, §5.4.3)
    ProductSDE(MaternSDE, CosineSDE) one band at $\omega_0$, width $\sim\lambda$ variability is concentrated in one band around a single frequency, with a phase that wanders the 40–50 day Madden–Julian oscillation in tropical winds Madden & Julian (1971); Foreman-Mackey et al. (2017)
    SumSDE of the above the sum you want the posterior of each component, not only of the total trend + seasonal + anomaly + noise decompositions Rasmussen & Williams (2006, §5.4.3)

    Two of these deserve a sentence each. Hasselmann's stochastic climate model treats a slow component (ocean temperature) as integrating fast weather forcing against a restoring feedback, which is exactly the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck SDE, so Matern-1/2 is the physically motivated null model for a mixed-layer anomaly rather than an arbitrary choice. The Mauna Loa CO₂ model in Rasmussen & Williams is a dense-GP sum of a long-term smooth trend, a periodic-times-decay seasonal term, medium-term irregularities and noise; in state-space form the same decomposition is SumSDE((MaternSDE(..., order=2), QuasiPeriodicSDE(...), MaternSDE(..., order=1))) plus a Gaussian likelihood, at linear cost in the record length. Their squared-exponential and rational-quadratic terms have no finite-dimensional SDE, which is why Matern blocks stand in for them here. Foreman-Mackey et al. reach the same band-limited class from the other direction: their celerite kernels are mixtures of stochastically driven damped harmonic oscillators, the stellar-variability analogue of the Matern × Cosine block.

    7.3 Time, space and the axis a kernel lives on¶

    Every kernel in this notebook is defined on one axis. That axis is usually time, and time is where the state-space form is strongest: it is causal, and irregular time stamps are handled exactly, because discretise_sequence takes each $\Delta t_k$ separately. Satellite overpasses with cloud gaps, or a buoy that drops out for a month, need no gridding or interpolation.

    A one-dimensional spatial coordinate works the same way: distance along an altimeter ground track, an aircraft or ship transect, or altitude in a vertical profile. The Markov property then runs along the transect; the filter has a direction, but the smoother uses both sides, so the posterior does not.

    For a field over 2-D or 3-D space and time there are two standard routes. The first keeps the SDE in time and puts a spatial kernel across locations, $k\big((\mathbf{s}, t), (\mathbf{s}', t')\big) = k_s(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}')\,k_t(t, t')$, so the Kalman state holds the whole spatial field at each time step (Särkkä, Solin & Hartikainen, 2013; Hamelijnck et al., 2021). The second writes a spatial Matern field as the solution of a stochastic PDE and discretises it into a sparse Gaussian Markov random field (Lindgren, Rue & Lindström, 2011); in pyrox that route belongs to pyrox_lgm. The limitation of the first route is separability: a product kernel cannot represent a signal that propagates, such as the annual-period westward Rossby waves that Schlax & Chelton (1994) found in North Atlantic altimetry. Propagating signals need a non-separable space-time covariance (Gneiting, 2002).

    7.4 Successes and failures to look out for¶

    Where these kernels do well.

    • Long, irregularly sampled records: the cost is $\mathcal{O}(N\,d^3)$, decades of hourly data are routine, and gaps cost nothing.
    • Decompositions: with a SumSDE, the smoother returns the posterior of each block (trend, season, anomaly) separately, so the components are interpretable without fitting them one after another.
    • Known frequencies: when physics fixes $\omega_k$, as for tides, a CosineSDE block constrains the signal far more tightly than any flexible kernel could.

    What to look out for.

    1. Smoothness mismatch. The squared-exponential (RBF) kernel has no finite-dimensional SDE and only an approximate state-space form (Hartikainen & Särkkä, 2010); Stein (1999) argues it is too smooth for most physical processes anyway. Matern is available only for $\nu \in \{1/2, 3/2, 5/2\}$, so check the observed spectral slope before choosing the order: an inertial-range turbulent signal, whose spectrum falls as $\omega^{-5/3}$ (Kolmogorov, 1941), is rougher than even Matern-1/2.
    2. Variance and lengthscale trade off. Under denser sampling of a fixed record, the variance and lengthscale of a Matern kernel cannot both be estimated consistently; only a combination of them can (Zhang, 2004). A short record constrains the slow components poorly, so put priors on $\ell$ and interpret the fitted variance together with it.
    3. Aliasing. A signal sampled less often than twice per period appears at a false, lower frequency. A CosineSDE at the true frequency still fits aliased data correctly, because it is evaluated at the true time stamps; a flexible kernel that lets the data choose the frequency will fit the alias instead. The figure below shows the classic case.
    4. A strictly periodic kernel where the cycle drifts. PeriodicSDE on its own has no diffusion: once its amplitude and phase are drawn, the cycle repeats exactly, so a cycle whose length or phase wanders lies outside its prior. Multiplying by a Matérn envelope removes that constraint: in both QuasiPeriodicSDE and Matern × CosineSDE the envelope broadens the spectral lines and lets phase coherence decay over the envelope's lengthscale (each nonzero harmonic of QuasiPeriodicSDE is itself a Matern × Cosine band). Choose between the two by harmonic content. QuasiPeriodicSDE keeps the periodic kernel's harmonics, for a non-sinusoidal cycle such as a seasonal cycle with a sharp peak; Matern × CosineSDE is a single band, for a near-sinusoidal oscillation such as the Madden–Julian oscillation.
    5. State dimension. Sharp cycle features need more harmonics $J$ (Solin & Särkkä, 2014), and a product multiplies state dimensions: Matern-5/2 × PeriodicSDE with $J = 10$ has $d = 3 \times 21 = 63$, so each filter step costs about $63^3$.
    6. Non-stationary or non-Gaussian variables. All these kernels are stationary. A trend whose rate changes needs a long-lengthscale Matern trend block, not a stationary anomaly kernel. Precipitation, counts and positive concentrations need a non-Gaussian likelihood on a latent Markov GP, which the non-Gaussian Markov notebook covers.
    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    # TOPEX/Poseidon's exact-repeat period, used by Schlax & Chelton (1994).
repeat_days = 9.9156


def alias_period_days(period_h: float, dt_days: float) -> float:
    """Apparent period of a sinusoid of ``period_h`` hours sampled every ``dt_days`` days."""
    f = 24.0 / period_h  # cycles per day
    cycles_per_sample = f * dt_days
    f_alias = abs(cycles_per_sample - round(cycles_per_sample)) / dt_days
    return 1.0 / f_alias


for name, period_h in tides_h.items():
    print(
        f"{name}: true period {period_h:7.4f} h  ->  alias period {alias_period_days(period_h, repeat_days):6.1f} d"
    )

t_fine = jnp.arange(0.0, 300.0, 1.0 / 48.0)  # half-hourly, 300 days
t_obs = jnp.arange(0.0, 300.0, repeat_days)
omega_m2 = 2.0 * jnp.pi * 24.0 / tides_h["M2"]
m2_true = jnp.cos(omega_m2 * t_fine)
m2_obs = jnp.cos(omega_m2 * t_obs)
p_alias = alias_period_days(tides_h["M2"], repeat_days)
# The alias is the sinusoid at the folded frequency that passes through the samples.
m2_alias = jnp.cos(2.0 * jnp.pi * t_fine / p_alias)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(13, 3.4))
ax.plot(
    t_fine,
    m2_true,
    color="0.75",
    lw=0.3,
    label="M2 tide (12.42 h), sampled half-hourly",
)
ax.plot(
    t_fine,
    m2_alias,
    color="C0",
    lw=1.6,
    label=f"what the samples show: a {p_alias:.1f}-day oscillation",
)
ax.plot(t_obs, m2_obs, "o", color="C3", ms=6, label=f"samples every {repeat_days} d")
ax.set_xlabel("time (days)")
ax.set_title("Aliasing: a 12.42-hour tide sampled on a 9.92-day repeat orbit")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=3)
ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.9)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
    # TOPEX/Poseidon's exact-repeat period, used by Schlax & Chelton (1994). repeat_days = 9.9156 def alias_period_days(period_h: float, dt_days: float) -> float: """Apparent period of a sinusoid of ``period_h`` hours sampled every ``dt_days`` days.""" f = 24.0 / period_h # cycles per day cycles_per_sample = f * dt_days f_alias = abs(cycles_per_sample - round(cycles_per_sample)) / dt_days return 1.0 / f_alias for name, period_h in tides_h.items(): print( f"{name}: true period {period_h:7.4f} h -> alias period {alias_period_days(period_h, repeat_days):6.1f} d" ) t_fine = jnp.arange(0.0, 300.0, 1.0 / 48.0) # half-hourly, 300 days t_obs = jnp.arange(0.0, 300.0, repeat_days) omega_m2 = 2.0 * jnp.pi * 24.0 / tides_h["M2"] m2_true = jnp.cos(omega_m2 * t_fine) m2_obs = jnp.cos(omega_m2 * t_obs) p_alias = alias_period_days(tides_h["M2"], repeat_days) # The alias is the sinusoid at the folded frequency that passes through the samples. m2_alias = jnp.cos(2.0 * jnp.pi * t_fine / p_alias) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(13, 3.4)) ax.plot( t_fine, m2_true, color="0.75", lw=0.3, label="M2 tide (12.42 h), sampled half-hourly", ) ax.plot( t_fine, m2_alias, color="C0", lw=1.6, label=f"what the samples show: a {p_alias:.1f}-day oscillation", ) ax.plot(t_obs, m2_obs, "o", color="C3", ms=6, label=f"samples every {repeat_days} d") ax.set_xlabel("time (days)") ax.set_title("Aliasing: a 12.42-hour tide sampled on a 9.92-day repeat orbit") ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=3) ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.9) ax.grid(alpha=0.25) fig.tight_layout() plt.show()
    M2: true period 12.4206 h  ->  alias period   62.1 d
S2: true period 12.0000 h  ->  alias period   58.7 d
K1: true period 23.9345 h  ->  alias period  173.2 d
O1: true period 25.8193 h  ->  alias period   45.7 d

    Every sample lies on the slow curve, so from the samples alone a 62-day oscillation and a 12.42-hour tide are indistinguishable. All the aliases printed above except K1's are shorter than 90 days, as Schlax & Chelton (1994) show for this orbit, so they sit in the same band as real intraseasonal ocean variability. The defence is the one in item 3: put the tide in the model as CosineSDE blocks at the astronomical frequencies and evaluate them at the true observation times.

    What this PR ships and what comes next¶

    PR 1 (issue #37 partial, #112 — already merged). The SDEKernel protocol and the MaternSDE family for $\nu \in \{1/2, 3/2, 5/2\}$.

    This PR (issue #37 finish). The kernel zoo on top of MaternSDE:

    • Primitives: ConstantSDE, CosineSDE (closed-form rotation discretise), PeriodicSDE (Solin & Sarkka 2014, Fourier-truncated MacKay periodic kernel via a stable log-space Bessel helper).
    • Composition rules: SumSDE (block-diagonal) and ProductSDE (Kronecker-sum drift, Kronecker-product readout / stationary covariance, with the diffusion matrix derived from the Lyapunov identity).
    • Convenience: QuasiPeriodicSDE as a documented ProductSDE(MaternSDE, PeriodicSDE).

    Next up — issue #38. MarkovGPPrior plus the Kalman filter / RTS smoother. Once that lands, every kernel above can be plugged directly into a NumPyro model with linear-time temporal inference: f = numpyro.sample("f", MarkovGPPrior(QuasiPeriodicSDE(...), times)).
